Making the most AI pilled company is the whole game:

1. make a second brain. one folder of markdown files on how you think, write and decide (obsidian)

2. talk to it. voice notes all day (wispr), and an agent files every fact, story and decision

3. make a company brain. customers, calls, numbers, pricing, playbooks, past decisions and why you made them

4. record every call and meeting (granola). the transcripts go straight into the brain

5. keep a facts file. true things about you and the company that agents are allowed to say. this kills made-up claims

6. keep a voice file. your 50 best posts, 20 you hate, and the words you never use

7. put all of it in git (github) so every change has a history

8. write one instruction file at the top (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). read these files before any task, never overwrite, always date

9. give agents memory across sessions so they stop starting from zero (claude-mem, mem0)

10. pipe every data source into one warehouse your agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). ads, analytics, CRM, payments

11. feed it data nobody else has. it's the only part a competitor can't download

the skills

12. don't start from zero. install the good ones first (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills)

13. grab the marketing ones too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills)

14. map every workflow in the company and rank them by money made or saved

15. do each one once while talking out loud, and record it

16. have an agent turn the recording into a skill. when to use it, the steps, the checks, the mistakes to avoid

17. one skill per job. small and boring beats one giant prompt

18. connect your tools with MCPs so agents can act and not only advise (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase)

19. give agents a browser (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome)

20. give agents a computer of their own for the tools with no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo)

21. give your best skills away in public. it's the new lead magnet

the agents

22. run an orchestrator that never turns off (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). it manages one agent per project, and each of those runs its own sub-agents

23. use coding agents for the building (claude code, codex, cursor, t3, antigravity)

24. wrap them in a harness so they plan, test and remember (ECC, superpowers)

25. manage the whole fleet in one place (paperclip). every agent gets a job, a budget and a log

26. put the skills on triggers (n8n, scheduled tasks). daily, weekly, on every new lead, on every cancellation

27. route your models (openrouter). the expensive one plans and checks (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), the cheap ones do the volume

28. cut the token bill. shorter outputs, smaller tool results (caveman)

29. run a local model for the data that can't leave your machine (gemma 4)

30. track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it

the factory

31. build the line. spec agent → builder agents in parallel (git worktrees) → test agent → reviewer agent → deploy (vercel, railway)

32. design goes through the same line (paper MCP), and a skill strips out anything that looks AI made (unslop)

33. every annoying task in the company becomes an internal tool by the end of the day

34. every customer request becomes a pull request before a human reads it (tstack for the PR workflow)

35. reviewer agents with a named bar. "would the best team in the world ship this?" reject until the answer is yes

36. keep 50 real cases with the right answer. rerun them every time a new model drops and switch to the winner

37. humans approve, own the outcome and talk to customers. that's the 10% you keep

the loop

38. every finished job writes back to the brain. what worked, what failed, what to stop doing

39. support tickets, analytics and social comments flow in every night

40. every friday an agent rewrites the playbooks from the week's results, and you approve the diff

41. every month, rank everything by profit per human hour. kill one thing and double one thing

the growth

42. research with agents before you spend a dollar (perplexity API, last30days skill)

43. outbound runs itself. find the leads, enrich, verify, send (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster)

44. send prospects finished work in place of a pitch

45. ads run on a loop. an agent writes the creative, publishes through the facebook ads API, kills the losers and scales the winners

46. agents make the creative too. images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs), music (lyria 3.5, suno)

47. turn every finished job into content. the story, the number, the prompt

48. every customer makes the brain smarter for the next one. that's your network effect

49. once it works, point it at a new niche. same agents, new context

The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

Acquire as much of it as you can, as fast as you can.

Build loops like this.

Anthropic just published an engineering guide on how to build always-on agents.

The biggest misconception: an always-on agent does NOT run 24/7. It sleeps almost all day, wakes up for short runs, saves state, and goes back to sleep.

The 5 core pieces I distilled:

1. Event Inbox
Put a database table between webhooks and your agent. Acknowledge webhooks fast, run only one active worker per user so runs never collide, and batch rapid messages together.

2. Timers
Keep timers in a separate table from the inbox. Split them into one-off follow-ups and recurring schedules. A background poller drops due timers into the inbox.

3. Lean Memory + Dreaming
Only store what cannot be looked up again: user instructions, user notes, past messages, and task progress. Load a small index at wakeup, not every file. Run periodic dreaming passes to clean out stale facts.

4. Unattended Permissions
Never put raw API keys inside the agent sandbox — inject them through an outside proxy. Use Deferred Tool Calls to pause risky actions for approval without blocking the worker.

5. Outbox
Queue outgoing replies so your agent paces notifications instead of spamming users at 3 AM.

I just finished talks about my software factories at two conferences. Afterwards a bunch of people came up and told me what they were surprised about. Here is a distillation of what people thought were hot takes from my two talks.

First hot take: I tell everyone to slow down. Most speakers go on about how fast they're going, but I strongly believe in pacing AI outputs to human speeds. I regularly tell AI-pilled CIOs and CTOs to chill: almost nobody is _actually_ going fast with AI. Engineering still moves at engineering speeds, and business moves even slower. The ones pushing too hard are starting to see downtime for it.

If you don't pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky.

My agents have, at times, overwhelmed my players with features, my accountant with emails, my merge queue with tickets, and my machines with load. Agents have pissed off my admins, resulting in name-calling, they've made messes in the game, and they've launched broken OSS without permission. The list goes on. 

I can get away with all this chaos because everyone involved in my operation is very forgiving. They're excited by the potential. But even so, I had to learn to slow down, real fast. And so that's what I preach.

Hot take #2: Should you buy a software factory? Do you even need one? No. You probably don't need one. Factories take an extraordinary amount of upkeep. They turn into garbage mountains unless you put a frightening amount of time and tokens into curating them. I had to burn my previous five factories down since it eventually became cheaper to rewrite them than to fix them. So I'm not out there advocating for software factories or swarms just yet. If you do want one, be aware that it is a significant commitment of both money and human leadership to keep one running.

Several people told me that I was the only one who stood up onstage, at either conference, and said Build, don't Buy. But my experience is that software factories grow to be highly bespoke to your domain. Mine is super tangled up with my game, and I think that's inevitable. Because the factory is not just building my product, it's supporting it too. It's a company in a box. And they're easy for Claude to build for you.

Third and arguably hottest take: Next year will have a lot of human/agent and agent/agent office drama, resulting from bringing in AI employees, and it will be gloriously funny, but also frustrating.

Many of you are already on this bandwagon, but everyone next year will have a personal chief-of-staff agent. Busy people, even hobbyists, will have whole entourages of helper agents. The hot take is that people will become so dependent on these little private entourages, that they'll bring them to work. Your people will talk to my people, etc. Whole protocols will emerge for private entourages negotiating work between humans, inside companies big and small.

Nearly all humans will wind up having to start working with AI employees next year, and it'll be the beginning of the biggest cultural change we've seen in a hundred years.

So that's the hot takes. Slow down. Only build a factory if you think you really need one. And focus on empowering yourself with your own agentic chief of staff (or team). Your entourage will define how you work with others, so start by perfecting how you work with them yourself.

this is a very important essay if you want to understand AI progress and how to measure it. i've been working on this for a few months now and i agree with almost everything here. here is a few additional (unstructured) thought:

--

1) slowdown factor: second order interactions in training LLMs

about ai progress that we see in math coming from ai research, i made a post about this exactly ~1 month ago and i totally agree, but one point i would add to dwarkesh's comment is that one thing that can slow down ai research progress is the number of "second order interactions"

i can't comment on what big labs know here, but at least in the open, it's really not clear how the full model training pipeline interacts together, and so even at each layer.

let's take pre-training and a change like making the KV cache smaller. it would allow us to hillclimb inference efficiency. many experiment as shown that this can be neutral (or even lead to gain) on validation loss, tho does it mean we get a better model for long context agentic tasks? lots of conflicting results here, minimax went from linear attention (M1) to full attention (M2) to sparse attention (M3), at the same time Kimi went from full attention (K1.5/K2) -> linear attention (K3). mistral large 4 found KV sharing hurts terminal bench 2 but not cross entropy, while dsv4.1 flash is one of the best small models and have an insane KV sharing pattern (only 1 layer computes KV on the decoder). most of the western oss model use SWA, most of the chinese oss one don't. this is only one example on a singular decision that have impact on everything else. in pre-training you can have different shape, arch, data, learning algorithm, tpp, scale, ect.. interacting together. and each of this element can also interact with mid and post training 

these are just a lot of possible interactions, i'd say much more than math, and as an automated researcher tries more changes the number of interactions will grow. compute remains the main bottleneck here, and there is a huge difference between closed american labs and the rest of the world.

important point is that there are ways to reduce compute needs in the "long term"* by finding better proxies, or spending more inference at the problem, i'm saying long term as it can be more intensive to find proxies at first since you need to validate them at scale and for that you need compute as well.

*long term here is not super long btw lol, some very random guess of mine would be that it can be months for oai/anthropic scale of compute, but maybe years for chinese labs for instance. there is also the question of how much the gap here change if frontier lab continue release their best model or not, i.e anthropic nerfing ai capabilities with mythos 5.2

--

2) data vs algorithm progress and how efficiency gain can be "misleading"

in general for training LLMs there are two types of improvements that you can make, either data or algorithmic

this is a big topic but imo the main difference is that data improvements feels much bigger partly because they are directly optimizing what we are measuring. i think everyone is familiar with benchmaxing but i'll take another example in pre-training

let's say you are measuring the CE on a mixture of held out documents (good example is the MAI paper here). the pre-training mixture that you are choosing will very naturally converge with the mixture of domains in the held out documents, and same for each domain (the different languages in code will be relatively similar to the ones you are evaluating against). if you are measuring between a random mixture with for instance less code because you care less about code (like older model from a few years ago), and one optimized for code, you will get INSANE efficiency gain. this is exactly what is happening in the magic blog that dwarkesh is citing. there is also the question of what held out document you have, i'm seeing a lot of new labs evaluating against their own held out codebase which are probably ai generated and hence would bias towards more synthetic data in pre-training for instance regardless of quality 

doesn't mean this is a bad way to do it, i'm just saying that this can be a bit misleading and that data and algorithm should be studied separately and we can't really compare those numbers imo

about algorithm, there are many more ways than looking at CE loss vs flops only btw. let's look at a niche example, say you are training on a giga large datacenter, you want a giga large batch size, so you need an architecture that is sample efficient at large batch size => you can go for matrix-based optimizers (can look at Muon/Adam T recently released that addresses this problem). this makes your efficiency gain being a plot with y axis loss, x axis batch size (it's more of a 3D plot btw as you still sweep flops/time for almost everything). you can also change the y axis and replace CE loss by smth else

-- 

3) about how we report and measure ai progress

about "ai having research taste" there is no benchmark for that, i've tried to do some effort here with my nanogpt experiment (have some newer results with newer model being more capable, just have to find the time to write a blog)

one interesting finding was how good anthropic models were compared to oai ones, and one of their biggest differentiating factors was navigating through the noise inherent to this bench and small scale ML experiment. i've also tried to test RL environments that teach "taste for things that scale", this was a side project and i didn't manage to make it work perfectly because it's a bit tricky to find the right scale and also quite compute intensive. but i'm 100% sure this is the way to go and something that anthropic/oai are currently training on, i'm really expecting this to work. also keep in mind that big labs have an insane database of experiments which happens to be extremely useful for creating such environments

one last thing here is that i think most labs right now are hesitating between reporting results to quantify progress and which intellectual property to release or not. @Sam_McCandlish made a post about that for the METR report and said that releasing metrics to quantify ai progress would accelerate other ai labs. while i disagree with this (you can see my answer there) i think this is a very important debate that should be discussed much more with different parties!

--

just some random thoughts that i had while watching the video, if everything goes well we should also release a lot more stuff regarding those topics soon at prime, i'm very very excited for this, hopefully this will create more useful data points for everyone to think about these very important topics!

v10 has changed from Icefish and Merope / Bladerunner to Quillfish, with mass production expected in 2029. MediaTek has won the design service order.

(1) Icefish is now v11, with mass production expected in 2030 and the design service order also going to MediaTek. Merope has lower visibility: no supplier has been chosen, and it may be canceled.

(2) MediaTek will be the sole supplier for v9 (Humufish & Triggerfish) and v10 (Quillfish), accounting for about 45–50%, 50–55%, and 55–60% of total TPU supply in 2027–2029, respectively. TPU’s contribution to its revenue and profit should rise each year.

Given limited initial production capacity, the v8 series should remain the bulk of TPU shipments through 2029. v8 is expected to be the main source of TPU profit growth for MediaTek and Broadcom over the next few years, thanks to significant accumulated learning-curve benefits and the fact that both handle procurement of key components and materials.

Its position as sole design supplier from v9 onward, together with a supply share that rises each year alongside TPU shipments, will expand its TPU revenue. Skills 2.0 is here!

(8x fewer tokens and 2x faster)

We package repeated workflows as skills all the time, but the agent still re-reads the skill and decides every step on every run, which costs tokens and time.

Devs just open-sourced Swamp, where your coding agent turns a repeated skill into a workflow that it builds once and runs again and again.

You describe the task once, and the agent breaks it into reusable behaviors connected in a workflow.

Every behavior has typed inputs and outputs, and plain code decides which step runs next. Swamp then gives you:

- model calls only on steps that need judgment
- secrets pulled from vaults and redacted from output
- versioned data from every run that you can query later
- a full record of what happened on each run

Here's the repo: https://t.co/GtaNpqAngp

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

Swamp plugs into the coding agent you already use, like:

- Claude Code
- Codex
- Cursor
- OpenCode
- And 5 more agent harnesses

In Swamp, the model is a step in the workflow, not the thing deciding what happens next.

The model steps still reason like any LLM call.

However, in this case, code owns the loop, so the agent doesn't spend tokens rediscovering the same process every time.

Here's an official result, where they turned a code-review skill into a Swamp workflow:

- Skill in Codex: about 4.6M tokens, 23 agents, 12.8 minutes
- Swamp workflow: about 506K tokens, 3 agents, 6.6 minutes

That is ~8x fewer tokens in about half the time, and most of the savings came from replacing the coordinator agent with plain code.

You can keep using skills while you prototype. Once a task starts repeating, ask your agent to turn it into a Swamp workflow.

This helps answer practical questions such as:

- Which steps actually need a model?
- What exactly happened on last week's run?
- Can a cheaper model handle the one step that needs judgment?

Once it's built, you can run the workflow from your agent, the CLI, a schedule, or an API, with every run recorded.

So you are no longer paying a model to figure out the same workflow on every run.

Instead, you spend tokens only on the steps where the model's judgment adds something.

The animation below shows how Swamp differs from Skills, and I worked with the team to put this together.

If you want to understand the coordination layer that Swamp replaces with code, I wrote a full breakdown of how Claude Code splits work across subagents and agent teams.

It covers when a single subagent is enough, when you need a team of agents that coordinate with each other, and what that coordination costs in context and tokens.

I stopped prompting AI for my videos. Now they come out better.

Here's why.

Most people have great ideas. What they don't have is great prompts. If your input is wrong, the output is wrong. If your input is generic, the output is generic. That's where most AI work dies.

Automation fixes this. You set the rules once, and the system does the prompting for you, the same way, every time.

That's what I love doing most in AI, and I think it's where most AI projects should put their energy.

Here's my own setup:
I build automations with CREAO, Claude Code and Grok Bot, and connect them to video platforms like Onsolo, Grok Imagine and Google Flow.

I don't prompt the character or the wardrobe. AI writes the script, prompts every shot, directs the scenes, merges the clips and adds the sound effects and theme music. The video comes out finished. No CapCut.

The same idea works in almost any niche:

→ Small business
Problem: You answer the same customer questions all day.
Automation: An agent replies from your price list and policies, then hands the tricky ones to you.

→ Content creators
Problem: You know what to post, but writing it daily burns you out.
Automation: One idea goes in. Posts for X, Instagram and LinkedIn come out in your voice, ready to schedule.

→ Online stores
Problem: Every new product needs a title, description and photos.
Automation: Upload a photo and the agent writes the listing, picks the keywords and formats it for your store.

→ Job seekers

→ Students and tutors
Problem: Revision materials take hours to make.
Automation: Drop in your notes and get a summary, flashcards and a practice quiz.

→ Researchers and founders
Problem: You can't read everything in your field every day.
Automation: An agent checks your sources each morning and sends you the five things that matter.

The tools are already here. The people who win are the ones who stop typing prompts one by one and start building systems that do it for them.

It is critically important that everyone thinking about AI become familiar with the term “handoverism.”

Many in the AI community believe that humanity should—or inevitably will—hand control of the world over to AI itself. Some view this not as a risk to be avoided, but as an outcome to be welcomed. Are we actually designing toward this future?

In his seminal essay, Machines of Loving Grace, CEO Dario Amodei contemplates:

“It could be a capitalist economy of AI systems, which then give out resources (huge amounts of them, since the overall economic pie will be gigantic) to humans based on some secondary economy of what the AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans (based on some judgment ultimately derived from human values).”

Are you prepared to receive your “resources” from an AI system, based on criteria it determines? The full title of the poem Dario borrowed the title from is "All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace." Do you want to be "watched over" by AI?

And if that belief informs Anthropic's corporate objectives, it belongs in the Risk Factors section of its S-1. It isn't there today.

I am decidedly anti-handoverism. I'm not here to tell you what your view should be. But I believe anyone making consequential decisions about AI—especially those drafting, advocating for, or enacting AI regulation—should be required to disclose where they stand on this fundamental question.
